Name: Adam Rich
Badge: Teacher as Researcher | Sustaining Literacy Routines
Looking back on this inquiry cycle, what did you learn about your teaching and your students that you might not have noticed otherwise? How did engaging in this teacher-research process shape or shift your thinking about your classroom practice?:

The biggest shift in my thinking was that research needs to be structured to allow students to form their opinions based on the evidence, rather than searching for information to support their view point. This concept is not new me, but the practical steps of instruction presented in these lessons showed me how to achieve that goal. I'm not sure that my students final writing hit the mark, partly because the topic of teen and technology carried a lot of baggage for middle school students. In the future, I would love to use this format with historical documents. I'm curious if students will develop more diverse responses to the topic in question. At the same time, one challenge will be correcting misunderstandings or false conclusions.

I can see many possibilities if these lesson are repeated throughout the year to add mini lessons on evaluating source credibility or weighing the merits of different kinds of evidence. These instructional topic support 21st century skills that all students will need as they gather information in the digital/AI age. I already use DBQs in my units, and this can better structure how I present those documents. The comments of my cohort brought to my attention the importance of cognitive load. Choosing manageable texts and spreading them out over multiple days allowed students to think deeply about each of them. The way I have been introducing documents can feel rushed, which leads students focus on task completion rather than text evaluation.

Think back to a moment during the lesson sequence that stands out. It could be a comment from a student, an unexpected challenge or success, a shift in engagement, or a moment when your own thinking changed. Describe what happened and why this moment feels meaningful to you now. What does it reveal:
Looking over my students note sheets revealed an interesting trend. Students generally had more detailed notes from the video than the two articles. Initially, I was worried they would struggle to write down specific facts from the video since they had to listen and write at the same time. But they did a good job listing important facts. They were less specific when they reflected on the articles. I wonder if using Kami to annotate instead of printing paper copies made a difference. The moment has me questioning how media type impacts student engagement.
As you look over the drafts your students produced in this lesson sequence, what early patterns, surprises, or questions are emerging for you? What aspects of your students’ writing are you most curious to explore more deeply with colleagues during our April regroup? What, if any, questions do you h:
Reflecting on my students finished drafts, I can say that most of them can locate relevant text evidence. However, their ability to introduce into their own writing to support an argument is varied. Common weaknesses include vague or incorrect references to text evidence, introducing their own opinions as evidence, or improperly introducing direct quotes and citing the source. I wonder if some these weakness reflect poor comprehension. How do I balance the need to let students wrestle with the text to develop their own opinion and the need to ensure they are correctly comprehending the author's claim and evidence. Based on what I am seeing, I definitely think I need some sort of mini lesson on ranking the value of piece of evidence from a text.
